title: Heat and Temperature
description: Grade 8 Physics: Heat and Temperature — concept notes, solved examples, key-point recaps, per-topic quizzes and free online tests.

topics.title: Heat and Temperature — The Difference
topics.concept:
In everyday language we often use the words "heat" and "temperature" as if they mean the same thing, but in science they are quite different. Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder one. It is the total energy of all the moving particles in an object. Temperature, on the other hand, is a measure of how hot or cold an object is — it tells us the degree of hotness, not the total energy. Heat is energy in transit; temperature is a number that tells us the hotness.

A key idea is that heat always flows from a body at higher temperature to a body at lower temperature, never the other way by itself. When a hot cup of tea is left in a room, heat flows from the hot tea to the cooler surroundings until both reach the same temperature. The flow of heat stops when the two objects reach the same temperature (called thermal equilibrium). So temperature decides the direction in which heat flows.

Heat and temperature have different SI units. The SI unit of heat is the joule (J), since heat is a form of energy (energy is measured in joules). The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K), though in everyday life we usually measure temperature in degrees Celsius (°C). So we say a cup of tea contains a certain amount of heat energy (in joules) and is at a certain temperature (in degrees Celsius or kelvin).

An important point is that temperature does not depend on the amount of substance, but heat does. For example, a small cup of boiling water and a large bucket of boiling water are at the same temperature (100 °C), but the large bucket contains much more heat energy, because it has many more hot particles. This is why the bucket can warm a room more than the cup, even though both are equally hot. Understanding that heat is energy and temperature is the degree of hotness, and that they have different units, is the foundation for studying thermometers, heat transfer, and the effects of heat in this chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
examples.solution:
Compare what each means.

  • Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter to a colder object.
  • Temperature is a measure of how hot or cold an object is (the degree of hotness).
  • Answer: Heat is a form of energy that flows from hot to cold; temperature measures how hot or cold an object is.
examples.answer: Heat is a form of energy that flows from hot to cold; temperature measures how hot or cold an object is.

examples.problem: Example 2: In which direction does heat flow between two objects?
examples.solution:
Recall the rule for heat flow.

  • Heat always flows from the object at higher temperature to the one at lower temperature.
  • It stops when both reach the same temperature.
  • Answer: Heat flows from the object at higher temperature to the one at lower temperature.
examples.answer: Heat flows from the object at higher temperature to the one at lower temperature.

examples.problem: Example 3: State the SI units of heat and temperature.
examples.solution:
Recall the correct units.

  • Heat is a form of energy, so its SI unit is the joule (J).
  • Temperature's SI unit is the kelvin (K), though we often use degrees Celsius (°C).
  • Answer: The SI unit of heat is the joule (J); the SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K).
examples.answer: The SI unit of heat is the joule (J); the SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K).

recap:
• Heat is a form of energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder one; temperature measures how hot or cold an object is.
  • Heat always flows from a higher temperature to a lower temperature, and stops when temperatures become equal.
  • The SI unit of heat is the joule (J); the SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K) (commonly measured in °C).
  • Temperature does not depend on the amount of substance, but the amount of heat does.
  • Two objects at the same temperature can contain very different amounts of heat (e.g. a cup vs a bucket of boiling water).

topics.title: Thermometers and Temperature Scales
topics.concept:
To measure temperature accurately, we use an instrument called a thermometer. Most common thermometers work on a simple principle: most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled. A thermometer usually contains a liquid (such as mercury or coloured alcohol) in a thin tube; when the temperature rises, the liquid expands and rises up the tube, and when it falls, the liquid contracts and goes down. The level of the liquid against a marked scale tells us the temperature.

There are different kinds of thermometers for different uses. A clinical thermometer is used to measure the temperature of the human body. It has a narrow range (because body temperature stays within narrow limits, around 37 °C) and a small "kink" (constriction) in the tube that stops the liquid from flowing back, so the reading can be taken after the thermometer is removed. A laboratory thermometer is used in science labs to measure a wider range of temperatures (for example, the temperature of liquids being heated); it has a longer scale and no kink. Modern digital thermometers display the temperature as a number on a screen.

Temperature is measured on different scales. The Celsius scale (°C) is the most commonly used everyday scale; on it, the freezing point of water is 0 °C and the boiling point of water is 100 °C (at normal pressure). The Fahrenheit scale (°F) is used in some countries; on it, water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F. The Kelvin scale (K) is the SI scale used in science; it starts from the lowest possible temperature, called absolute zero (0 K), and on it water freezes at 273 K and boils at 373 K. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.

These three scales — Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin — are simply different ways of numbering the same temperatures, much like measuring length in different units. Because they are related in fixed ways, a temperature given on one scale can be converted to another using conversion formulas (which we study in the next topic). Understanding thermometers — how they use expansion, the types for body and lab use, and the Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin scales — lets us measure and compare temperatures precisely.

examples.problem: Example 1: On what principle does a common thermometer work?
examples.solution:
Recall how a liquid thermometer responds to heat.

  • Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled.
  • A thermometer's liquid expands and rises (or contracts and falls) with temperature, showing the reading on a scale.
  • Answer: A common thermometer works on the principle that a liquid expands when heated and contracts when cooled.
examples.answer: A common thermometer works on the principle that a liquid expands when heated and contracts when cooled.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between a clinical and a laboratory thermometer?
examples.solution:
Compare their uses and ranges.

  • A clinical thermometer measures human body temperature, has a narrow range, and a kink to hold the reading.
  • A laboratory thermometer measures a wider range of temperatures and has no kink.
  • Answer: A clinical thermometer (narrow range, with a kink) measures body temperature; a laboratory thermometer (wide range, no kink) measures a broader range.
examples.answer: A clinical thermometer (narrow range, with a kink) measures body temperature; a laboratory thermometer (wide range, no kink) measures a broader range.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give the freezing and boiling points of water on the Celsius scale.
examples.solution:
Recall the fixed points on the Celsius scale.

  • On the Celsius scale, the freezing point of water is 0 °C.
  • The boiling point of water is 100 °C (at normal pressure).
  • Answer: On the Celsius scale, water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
examples.answer: On the Celsius scale, water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.

recap:
• A thermometer measures temperature; common ones work on the principle that a liquid expands when heated and contracts when cooled.
  • A clinical thermometer measures human body temperature (narrow range around 37 °C, with a kink to hold the reading).
  • A laboratory thermometer measures a wider range of temperatures (longer scale, no kink); digital thermometers show a number.
  • The Celsius scale: water freezes at 0 °C, boils at 100 °C. The Fahrenheit scale: 32 °F and 212 °F. The Kelvin scale: 273 K and 373 K.
  • The three scales are different ways of numbering the same temperatures; a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.

topics.title: Conversion of Temperature Between Scales
topics.concept:
Since temperature can be measured on the Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F), and Kelvin (K) scales, we often need to convert a temperature from one scale to another. This is just like converting between units of length. The three scales are related by fixed formulas, because they are different ways of numbering the same temperatures. Knowing the conversions lets us understand a temperature given on any scale.

The relationship between the three scales can be written as a single combined formula: C / 5 = (F − 32) / 9 = (K − 273) / 5 Here C is the Celsius temperature, F is the Fahrenheit temperature, and K is the Kelvin temperature. From this combined relation, we can pick out the formula we need for any particular conversion. The numbers 5, 9, 32, and 273 come from the fixed points (freezing and boiling of water) on each scale.

To convert between Celsius and Fahrenheit, we use C/5 = (F − 32)/9. From this, to go from Celsius to Fahrenheit: F = (9/5) × C + 32, and to go from Fahrenheit to Celsius: C = (5/9) × (F − 32). For example, to convert 100 °C to Fahrenheit: F = (9/5) × 100 + 32 = 180 + 32 = 212 °F — which is correct, since water boils at both 100 °C and 212 °F.

To convert between Celsius and Kelvin, the relation is simpler because the scales differ only by a shift of 273 (their degrees are the same size): K = C + 273 and C = K − 273. For example, 0 °C = 0 + 273 = 273 K (freezing point of water), and 27 °C = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Using these formulas — C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5 — we can change any temperature from one scale to another, allowing us to compare and understand temperatures measured on different scales.

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the combined formula relating the Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin scales.
examples.solution:
Recall the relation between the three scales.

  • The three temperature scales are related by a single combined formula.
  • It is C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5.
  • Answer: C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5.

recap:
• The Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin scales are related by: C/5 = (F − 32)/9 = (K − 273)/5.
  • Celsius to Fahrenheit: F = (9/5) × C + 32; Fahrenheit to Celsius: C = (5/9) × (F − 32).
  • Celsius to Kelvin: K = C + 273; Kelvin to Celsius: C = K − 273.
  • The Celsius and Kelvin scales differ only by a shift of 273 (their degrees are the same size).
  • These formulas let any temperature be converted from one scale to another.

quiz.explanation: F = (9/5) × C + 32 converts Celsius to Fahrenheit.

100 °C in Fahrenheit is:

topics.title: Transfer of Heat — Conduction, Convection, and Radiation
topics.concept:
Heat, being a form of energy, can travel (transfer) from one place to another. There are three ways in which heat is transferred: conduction, convection, and radiation. Each works differently and is important in different situations. Understanding these three modes explains how a metal spoon gets hot in tea, how a room warms up, and how heat from the Sun reaches the Earth across empty space.

Conduction is the transfer of heat through a solid without the substance itself moving. When one end of a solid is heated, the particles there vibrate faster and pass their energy to neighbouring particles, so heat travels through the material from the hot end to the cold end. Metals are good conductors of heat (which is why a metal spoon in hot tea soon becomes hot to hold), while wood, plastic, and air are poor conductors (insulators). Conduction is the main way heat moves through solids.

Convection is the transfer of heat in liquids and gases (fluids) by the actual movement of the heated fluid. When a fluid is heated, the warm part becomes less dense and rises, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place; this sets up circulating convection currents that carry heat throughout the fluid. Convection explains how water heats up in a pan, how a room is warmed by a heater, and how sea breezes and winds form. It cannot occur in solids, because their particles cannot move freely.

Radiation is the transfer of heat without any medium, by means of invisible heat rays (a kind of energy wave). Radiation is the only way heat can travel through a vacuum (empty space). This is how heat from the Sun reaches the Earth across the empty space, and how we feel the warmth of a fire or a hot object without touching it. Dark, dull surfaces absorb and emit radiation well, while shiny, light surfaces reflect it. So heat travels by conduction (through solids), convection (through moving fluids), and radiation (through space without a medium) — three modes that together explain the movement of heat all around us.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three ways in which heat is transferred.
examples.solution:
Recall the three modes of heat transfer.

  • Heat travels through solids by conduction.
  • It travels through fluids by convection, and through space by radiation.
  • Answer: The three ways are conduction, convection, and radiation.
examples.answer: The three ways are conduction, convection, and radiation.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does heat travel by conduction?
examples.solution:
Recall conduction in solids.

  • When a solid is heated, its particles vibrate faster and pass energy to neighbouring particles.
  • So heat travels through the solid from the hot end to the cold end, without the substance moving.
  • Answer: In conduction, heated particles in a solid pass energy to neighbouring particles, so heat travels through the solid from hot to cold.
examples.answer: In conduction, heated particles in a solid pass energy to neighbouring particles, so heat travels through the solid from hot to cold.

examples.problem: Example 3: By which mode of heat transfer does the Sun's heat reach the Earth, and why?
examples.solution:
Consider what lies between the Sun and Earth.

  • The space between the Sun and the Earth is a vacuum (no medium).
  • Only radiation can transfer heat without a medium, so the Sun's heat reaches us by radiation.
  • Answer: The Sun's heat reaches the Earth by radiation, because radiation can travel through the vacuum of space without a medium.
examples.answer: The Sun's heat reaches the Earth by radiation, because radiation can travel through the vacuum of space without a medium.

recap:
• Heat is transferred in three ways: conduction, convection, and radiation.
  • Conduction is heat transfer through a solid by particles passing energy to neighbours, without the solid moving; metals are good conductors, wood and plastic are insulators.
  • Convection is heat transfer in liquids and gases by the actual movement of the heated fluid (warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks), forming convection currents.
  • Radiation is heat transfer without any medium, by invisible heat rays; it is the only mode that works through a vacuum.
  • The Sun's heat reaches the Earth by radiation; dark dull surfaces absorb/emit radiation well, while shiny surfaces reflect it.

quiz.explanation: Conduction is heat transfer through a solid by particles passing energy.

quiz.q: Heat transfer in liquids and gases by the movement of the fluid is called:
quiz.explanation: Convection transfers heat by the actual movement of the heated fluid.

quiz.q: Heat transfer that needs no medium and can occur through a vacuum is:
quiz.explanation: Radiation needs no medium and is the only mode that works through a vacuum.

quiz.q: The Sun's heat reaches the Earth mainly by:
quiz.explanation: The Sun's heat crosses the vacuum of space by radiation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good conductor of heat?
quiz.explanation: Metals are good conductors of heat; wood, plastic, and air are insulators.

topics.title: Thermal Expansion, Specific Heat, and Latent Heat
topics.concept:
When substances are heated, several important effects occur. The first is thermal expansion: most substances expand (increase in size) when heated and contract (decrease in size) when cooled. This happens because heating makes the particles vibrate more and move slightly farther apart. Solids, liquids, and gases all expand on heating, with gases expanding the most and solids the least. Thermal expansion has many practical effects: gaps are left between railway tracks and in bridges to allow for expansion in hot weather, and electric and telephone wires are left slightly loose so they do not snap when they contract in winter.

A useful application of the expansion of solids is the bimetallic strip. This is made of two different metals joined together, which expand by different amounts when heated. As a result, the strip bends when its temperature changes. This bending is used in thermostats — devices that switch heating or cooling appliances on and off automatically to control temperature — and in fire alarms. So the simple fact that metals expand differently is put to clever use.

The second effect involves how much heat different substances need to warm up, described by specific heat capacity. Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of a substance by 1 degree. Different substances have different specific heats — water has a very high specific heat, meaning it needs a lot of heat to warm up and releases a lot when it cools. The heat required is given by Q = m c ΔT, where Q is the heat, m is the mass, c is the specific heat capacity, and ΔT is the temperature change. The high specific heat of water explains why it is used as a coolant, and why sea breezes occur (land heats and cools faster than the sea).

The third effect is latent heat, the heat involved in changing the state of a substance (melting or boiling) without changing its temperature. When ice melts into water, or water boils into steam, heat is absorbed but the temperature stays the same during the change — this absorbed heat is the latent heat. The heat needed to melt a solid into a liquid is the latent heat of fusion, and the heat needed to change a liquid into a gas is the latent heat of vaporisation. Latent heat plays a big role in climate (for example, when water evaporates and condenses) and in why steam burns are so severe. So thermal expansion, specific heat, and latent heat together describe the rich variety of effects that heat produces, completing our study of heat and temperature.

examples.solution:
Recall the effect of heat on size.

  • Most substances expand (increase in size) when heated and contract when cooled.
  • This is because heating makes the particles vibrate more and move slightly farther apart.
  • Answer: Thermal expansion is the increase in size of a substance when it is heated (and contraction when cooled).
examples.answer: Thermal expansion is the increase in size of a substance when it is heated (and contraction when cooled).

examples.problem: Example 2: Calculate the heat needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 °C. (Specific heat of water c = 4200 J/kg°C.)
examples.solution:
Use Q = m c ΔT.

  • m = 2 kg, c = 4200 J/kg°C, ΔT = 10 °C.
  • Q = m c ΔT = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84,000 J.
  • Answer: The heat needed is 84,000 J (84 kJ).
examples.answer: The heat needed is 84,000 J (84 kJ).

examples.solution:
Recall the heat involved in a change of state.

  • Latent heat is the heat absorbed (or released) when a substance changes state (melting or boiling).
  • During the change, the heat is absorbed but the temperature does not change.
  • Answer: Latent heat is the heat involved in changing the state of a substance without changing its temperature.
examples.answer: Latent heat is the heat involved in changing the state of a substance without changing its temperature.

recap:
• Thermal expansion: most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled (gases expand most, solids least); gaps are left in railway tracks and bridges for this.
  • A bimetallic strip (two metals that expand differently) bends on heating and is used in thermostats and fire alarms.
  • Specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree; heat required is Q = m c ΔT.
  • Water has a high specific heat capacity, which is why it warms and cools slowly and why sea breezes occur.
  • Latent heat is the heat absorbed/released when a substance changes state (melting/boiling) without a change in temperature — latent heat of fusion (solid→liquid) and of vaporisation (liquid→gas).
